blocks.text: **The task.** An array of N+1 integers holds values in the range 1 to N. Exactly one value repeats. Find it **without modifying the array** and using O(1) space.
Why the usual tricks are blocked
The constraints deliberately close every easy door. A hash set is O(N) space. Sorting modifies the array. Negation marking also modifies it. Cyclic sort modifies it too.
What remains is a genuinely clever reframing.
The array as a linked list
Read each value as a **pointer to the next index**. Starting anywhere, `i -> nums[i] -> nums[nums[i]] -> ...` traces a path through the array.

Because values are in 1..N and there are N+1 slots, this path can never leave the array — so it must eventually revisit a position. It forms a **cycle**. And the entry point of that cycle is exactly the duplicated value, because two different indices point into it.
The problem is now "find where a linked list cycle begins", solvable with a slow and a fast pointer in O(1) space.

This is the part that looks like magic. The short version: when the pointers first meet, the distance from the array's start to the cycle entrance equals the distance from the meeting point to that entrance, going around.

So resetting one pointer to the start and advancing both at the same speed makes them meet precisely at the entrance. It falls out of the algebra of the two distances, and it is worth deriving once on paper.
**Time: O(N)**, **Space: O(1)**, and the array is untouched — satisfying all three constraints at once.
If the problem ever drops the no-modification rule, use cyclic sort instead. It is far easier to reason about.
